opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about data for robotics as a kind of pyramid, and internet data sits at the very bottom. It's the base layer, and it's the largest in volume by far.

The strength is obvious: scale and diversity. There are billions of hours of video on YouTube and elsewhere showing humans doing every task you could imagine. People cook, fold laundry, fix cars, assemble furniture, play sports. All of that encodes a tremendous amount of common sense about how the physical world works. Objects fall when you drop them. Liquids pour. Doors swing on hinges. You grasp a mug by the handle. Then there's the text and image data that gave us large language and vision-language models. That gives a robot semantic understanding, so it knows what a "spatula" is or what "tidy up the kitchen" means. So internet data is fantastic for building priors: perception, language grounding, a rough intuitive physics, and high-level planning.

The limitation is just as fundamental, though. Internet data has no action labels. When you watch a video of someone flipping a pancake, you see pixels changing, but you don't get the motor commands. You don't know the joint angles, the torques, the forces at the fingertips, or the closed-loop corrections happening at hundreds of hertz. And robotics is ultimately about outputting those actions. There's also an embodiment gap. Human hands and bodies are not the same as a robot's grippers or a humanoid's actuators, so even if you could extract human motion, it doesn't map one-to-one. And the data is passive. It's observational and never interactive, so the model never gets to try something, fail, and learn from the consequences.

So you can't train a robot foundation model on internet data alone, the way you largely can for an LLM. That's why I think you need the other layers of the pyramid. In the middle is simulation and synthetic data, where you get actions and physics for free and can scale with compute rather than human time. At the top is real-robot data, collected through teleoperation. That's the highest quality, perfectly in-distribution for the hardware, but it's extremely expensive and limited. Humans can only teleoperate for so many hours a day, and robots break.

The real art is figuring out how to blend these. You use the internet for breadth and common sense, simulation for scale and action-rich experience, and real data to close the gap to reality. No single source is sufficient, and I think anyone who bets on just one of them is going to hit a wall.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says internet data has no action labels and lists motor commands, joint angles, torques, and forces as missing signals.

fable-5.1.text:
Internet data is this incredible gift, and it's also a trap, and you have to hold both of those in your head at the same time.

The gift part is obvious. We have billions of videos of humans doing things. People cooking, folding laundry, assembling furniture, opening doors, pouring water. That is, in some sense, the largest demonstration dataset of embodied behavior that has ever existed. And the thing we learned from language models is that scale plus diversity is what gets you the magic. So when you look at YouTube, you think, this is the corpus. This is the Common Crawl for robotics.

And there's real signal in there. A video model trained on that data learns physics. It learns that cups fall when you let go, that liquids pour, that doors swing on hinges. It learns object permanence, affordances, how humans sequence a task. It learns what a kitchen looks like, what a factory floor looks like. All of that commonsense world knowledge is exactly what a robot needs and exactly what you cannot possibly collect by teleoperation at scale. So the priors are there.

Now the trap. Internet video has no action labels. You see the pixels change, but you never see the motor torques, the joint angles, the gripper commands that caused it. It's observation without actuation. And the human body is not a robot body. A human hand has twenty-something degrees of freedom and tendons and skin with incredibly dense tactile sensing. A robot hand doesn't. So even when you see a human do something perfectly, there's an embodiment gap you have to bridge. The video tells you what, it doesn't tell you how, at least not in a form a robot can execute.

The second limitation is that it's third-person and curated. People film the interesting parts. Nobody uploads forty minutes of fumbling to grasp a slippery object. Robots need the failures, the recoveries, the boring contact-rich moments, and those are systematically underrepresented.

So my view is you treat internet data as a pretraining substrate, not the whole meal. It gives you the world model, the visual and physical commonsense. Then you need a second layer: real robot data, which is expensive and slow but has the actions in it, and simulation, which is cheap and has perfect labels but has its own reality gap. I think of it as a data pyramid. Internet at the bottom, massive and cheap. Simulation in the middle. Real-world teleoperation at the top, small and precious. The foundation model has to drink from all three, and the research question is really how you align them so that what the model learns from watching humans transfers into something the robot can actually do.

r001.rationale: The response describes internet videos of people performing tasks as a large demonstration source and says they teach physics and other commonsense world knowledge useful to robots.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says internet video lacks action labels and does not show motor torques, joint angles, or gripper commands.

astra-6.text:
Internet data gives us a tremendous amount of semantic knowledge. You can learn what objects are, what people typically do with them, and what a successful task looks like. If I ask a robot to clean up a kitchen, that prior knowledge is incredibly useful. We shouldn’t have to teach it the meaning of every object from scratch.

But the internet mostly shows you what the world looks like. It doesn’t give you the full interaction loop. A video of someone picking up a cup doesn’t tell you the forces on their fingers, the friction at the contact points, or exactly how they adjusted when the cup started slipping. And it doesn’t tell you what would have happened if they had taken a different action.

So I think internet data is a very powerful starting point, but it’s not sufficient on its own. A robot needs experience connecting actions to consequences—through robot demonstrations, simulation, and interaction with the physical world. The challenge is turning broad knowledge about the world into reliable control within it.

sol-6.1.text:
Internet data gives us this incredible breadth of knowledge. You can learn what objects are, how people talk about tasks, and even the rough steps involved in cooking a meal or assembling furniture. So I think it’s a very powerful starting point for a robot foundation model.

But there’s a fundamental gap: the internet mostly records what the world looks like and what people say about it. A robot needs to know what happens when it acts. If I apply this much force, will the cup move, slip, or break? Video usually doesn’t give you the forces, the tactile feedback, or the precise actions that produced the motion.

And the data is biased toward what humans find worth recording. We have lots of successful demonstrations, but much less coverage of all the little failures and corrections that make physical skills robust.

So I see internet data as giving the robot a broad prior about the world. You still need grounded experience—from robot demonstrations, simulation, and interaction—to connect that knowledge to actions and their consequences.

r001.rationale: It describes internet data broadly and mentions video, but does not identify online instructional videos as the source of physical common-sense priors.

r002.rationale: It says video usually lacks the precise actions that produced motion, conveying the absence of robot action signals such as motor-control commands.
